case_name: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v. Tech Square Engineering Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
holding_summary: Reversing a 2023 Single Judge finding that Toyota had not proven Indian use or reputation in the mark ALPHARD predating Tech Square's 2015 'proposed to be used' registration, a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that unsolicited grey-market imports, online listings and press coverage since 2008 were sufficient to establish trans-border reputation in India. The Court declared ALPHARD a well-known trade mark and ordered cancellation of Tech Square's Indian registrations, holding that in luxury/niche markets brand visibility and global reputation — not mass local penetration — drive consumer recognition.
why_it_matters: Foreign brand owners without direct Indian sales now have a clearer, DHC-endorsed evidentiary path — grey-market presence, online visibility and press coverage — to establish trans-border reputation and defeat squatted registrations of niche or luxury marks in India.

case_name: D.P. Jain Bangalore Chennai Expressways Pvt. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India
holding_summary: Under a Concession Agreement dated 4 February 2022 for a section of the Bangalore-Chennai Expressway, a Division Bench had on 20 August 2026 partly allowed D.P. Jain's appeal, declaring the project eligible for free fly ash with transportation and referring its monetary claim (including Rs. 180.16 crore) to the Dispute Resolution Board/Arbitral Tribunal for quantification. After NHAI declined to implement that ruling and terminated the Concession Agreement on 1 September 2026, Justice Sachin Datta of the Delhi High Court, on 10 September 2026, constituted a three-member Arbitral Tribunal after both parties agreed to depart from the SAROD arbitration procedure prescribed in their agreement.
why_it_matters: Concessionaires facing an authority's non-implementation of a favourable court ruling, followed by termination of the concession, can secure a substitute tribunal by consent even where the contract mandates a specific institutional arbitration mechanism like SAROD.

case_name: Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax (Central)-2 v. M/S Delhivery Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: The Revenue had disallowed Delhivery's claimed deduction of Rs. 51.48 crore for ESOP expenditure and made an addition under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, on the ground that the share valuation supporting the ESOP had been prepared by a Chartered Accountant rather than a merchant banker. A Delhi High Court bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta upheld the deduction, holding that a CBDT order permitted CA-prepared valuations at the relevant time and that a later rule requiring merchant-banker valuation could not be applied retrospectively to reject it.
why_it_matters: Companies that claimed ESOP expenditure deductions using contemporaneous Chartered Accountant valuations have a strong precedent to resist reassessment where the Revenue seeks to apply a later, stricter valuation-methodology requirement retrospectively.

case_name: MITC Rolling Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/S. Renuka Realtors & Ors.
holding_summary: MITC Rolling Mills had filed Commercial Suit No. 06 of 2021 before the District Judge, Nashik, seeking recovery of over Rs. 2.52 crore for supply of TMT/Fe-500 material; when its plaint was rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, the Bombay High Court held that no appeal lay against that order under Section 13(1A) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. The Supreme Court, per Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta, set that aside, holding that rejection of a plaint is a 'decree' under Section 2(2) CPC and is therefore appealable under the main part of Section 13(1A), with the proviso restricting only appeals against purely interlocutory orders.
why_it_matters: Commercial litigants whose plaint has been rejected under Order VII Rule 11 now have settled confirmation that a first appeal lies as of right under the Commercial Courts Act, removing an uncertainty that previously varied across High Courts.

case_name: Industria de Diseño Textil, S.A. v. Registrar of Trade Marks & Anr.
holding_summary: Inditex, owner of the ZARA mark, appealed the Trade Marks Registry's refusal to cancel a third party's registration of ZORA (Registration No. 4310686 in Class 24). Justice Jyoti Singh held that a mark need not first be formally declared 'well-known' under Section 11(6)-(9) before its owner can invoke the cross-category protection in Section 11(2) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and, applying the anti-dissection rule, found ZORA phonetically and structurally similar enough to ZARA that its adoption was without due cause and would take unfair advantage of ZARA's distinctive character and repute. The Court ordered cancellation of the ZORA registration and directed the Registrar to remove it from the Register within two months.
why_it_matters: Owners of globally recognised brands do not need a separate, formal 'well-known mark' declaration in hand before invoking Section 11(2) to block a similar mark in an unrelated goods category — reputation and distinctiveness evidence placed before the court can suffice on its own.

case_name: M/s Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Suryakand D. Lad & Ors.
holding_summary: Workers engaged through a contractor at ONGC claimed gratuity directly from ONGC as principal employer; the Controlling Authority under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 and, on appeal, the Bombay High Court had held ONGC liable to pay. A bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and Manmohan set that aside, holding that a Controlling Authority's jurisdiction under the Act is limited to computing the gratuity due to an already-established employee — it has no power to first adjudicate the disputed, anterior question of who the real employer is. Since ONGC had already paid the workers the disputed amount, the Court directed that no recovery be made from them.
why_it_matters: Principal employers facing a gratuity claim from contract workers should raise the employer-identity dispute at the earliest stage and be prepared to contest jurisdiction, since a Controlling Authority's order fixing them as the liable employer is now vulnerable to challenge as being outside its statutory power to decide.

case_name: Securities and Exchange Board of India v. Vedanta Limited & Ors.
holding_summary: Vedanta had announced a buyback of 17.09 crore equity shares at up to Rs. 335 per share but ultimately bought back only about 3.67 crore shares for Rs. 1,225.45 crore; SEBI alleged the announcement was misleading and made without genuine intent to complete it, invoking the PFUTP Regulations, while Vedanta argued SEBI's own release of its buyback escrow showed there was no fraud. A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan held that release of the cash escrow deposited under Regulation 15B(8) of the Buyback Regulations does not bar a separate, independent fraud inquiry under the PFUTP Regulations, but remanded the fraud question itself to the Securities Appellate Tribunal for fresh decision within six months, since neither the Adjudicating Officer nor SAT had engaged with disputed discrepancies in the underlying trading data.
why_it_matters: Companies cannot treat SEBI's release of a buyback escrow as closing the door on fraud scrutiny of the same buyback announcement — a PFUTP inquiry into the company's true intent at the time of announcement can proceed independently and on its own evidentiary track.

case_name: Pr. Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-1, Delhi v. Patanjali Ayurved Ltd. (and connected appeals)
citation: ITA Nos. (batch of 7 appeals, AYs 2013-14 to 2015-16 and 2017-18)
holding_summary: Seven income-tax appeals concerning Patanjali Ayurved — four filed by the assessee and three by the Revenue, argued and reserved on different dates in August 2025 — were disposed of by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal through a single common order running to fewer than seven paragraphs, without engaging with the assessee's contentions or the distinct issues raised in each appeal. A Delhi High Court Division Bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta quashed all seven ITAT orders, describing the Tribunal's disposal as reflecting 'undue haste' and 'recklessness' and as bereft of logic, reasoning or rationale, and directed that the matters be reheard afresh by a differently constituted ITAT bench.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers and the Revenue alike now have a clear precedent that a Tribunal cannot dispose of multiple, factually and legally distinct appeals through one cursory common order — a party facing an unreasoned or rushed ITAT disposal has a strong basis to seek its quashing on writ or appeal.

case_name: I.S.D.S. Private Limited v. M/s Khemka Food Products Private Limited
citation: Supreme Court of India (referred to a larger Bench)
holding_summary: Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 bars the institution of specified trademark suits before any court inferior to a District Court, yet several High Courts, exercising powers under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, have notified Courts of Civil Judge (Senior Division) as Commercial Courts for disputes within particular pecuniary limits — including trademark suits. A bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran found an apparent conflict between the two statutory regimes and referred to a larger Bench the question whether a State notification under the Commercial Courts Act can empower a Civil Judge below the District Court to hear trademark infringement suits, so that the law can be applied uniformly across states.
why_it_matters: Trademark litigants across India face inconsistent answers, state by state, on whether their infringement suit can validly be heard by a Commercial Court judge below District Court rank — this reference should produce a single, nationwide rule on which forum has jurisdiction.

case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Smt. Thungala Dhana Laxmi & Ors.
holding_summary: Examining non-compliance with Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (mandatory third-party insurance) and inconsistent motor policy structures across insurers, a bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Prashant Kumar Mishra held that a comprehensive/package motor policy covers vehicle occupants and cannot be equated with a bare third-party policy. Finding that 56% of vehicles on Indian roads are uninsured, the Court issued nationwide directions including ANPR-linked automatic e-challans for uninsured vehicles, a fuel-insurance linkage pilot, and extension of mandatory third-party cover from one year to four years for new cars and six years for new two-wheelers, with compliance affidavits due from stakeholders and further review hearings to follow.
why_it_matters: Vehicle owners will need to budget for a longer, prepaid block of mandatory third-party insurance at the time of purchase, and insurers/regulators face court-mandated enforcement infrastructure (ANPR e-challans, fuel-linkage) aimed at closing India's large uninsured-vehicle gap.

case_name: Anup Vikal & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
holding_summary: An Internal Committee, on a POSH complaint filed by an employee in October 2023, communicated that the allegations did not contain a 'sexual element' and therefore fell outside its jurisdiction; the Industrial Court later went further and set aside the IC's communication on merits, remanding the complaint for a fresh inquiry. The Bombay High Court held that an IC's threshold determination that a complaint lacks a sexual element and warrants no inquiry is itself a 'recommendation' under Section 13(2) of the POSH Act and is therefore appealable under Section 18, upheld the appeal's maintainability on that basis, but set aside the Industrial Court's own merits findings and remanded the matter with directions to decide only whether the complaint contains an element of sexual harassment.
why_it_matters: An employee whose sexual harassment complaint is summarily rejected at the threshold by an Internal Committee is not left without recourse — that threshold rejection itself can be appealed under Section 18 of the POSH Act, rather than requiring a fresh complaint or writ petition.

case_name: CG Tollway Ltd. v. Union of India
citation: Rajasthan High Court judgment under Supreme Court appeal (notice issued 3 September 2026)
court: Rajasthan High Court; on appeal before the Supreme Court of India
holding_summary: CG Tollway, a BOT concessionaire operating a national highway stretch, contested a GST demand exceeding Rs. 16.36 crore on the ground that its right to collect toll from road users was not 'consideration' for the construction services it rendered to NHAI. A Division Bench of the Rajasthan High Court held that the concessionaire had received commercially valuable rights (the toll-collection right) in place of direct monetary payment, that the arrangement bore the characteristics of a barter transaction, and upheld the GST demand with interest and penalty as taxable consideration for works-contract services. CG Tollway has appealed to the Supreme Court, which issued notice and an interim stay application on 3 September 2026 without expressing any view on the merits.
why_it_matters: BOT/HAM concessionaires and their lenders across the highway, airport, port and mining PPP sectors face a live risk that toll or other collection rights granted under a concession agreement could be treated as taxable GST consideration for the underlying construction — a Supreme Court ruling either way will directly affect how such projects are bid, financed and priced.

case_name: Arth Micro Finance Private Ltd. & Ors. v. Shivalik Small Finance Bank Ltd.
citation: 2026 INSC 1014; Civil Appeal No. 13015 of 2026 (arising out of SLP (C) No. 26596 of 2026)
holding_summary: Shivalik Small Finance Bank had constituted an arbitral tribunal against Arth Micro Finance and its guarantors, who objected that the tribunal had close links to the bank and that its appointment lacked their proven consent. A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran held that an arbitral tribunal's appointment without proven consent of the opposite party, made in the face of a bias objection, is non est in law and renders the initiation of arbitration itself invalid. The Court set aside a High Court order that had dismissed the borrower's challenge on the technical ground of limitation, quashed three coercive interim orders passed by the tribunal, and directed immediate restoration of properties and restitution of funds.
why_it_matters: The ruling gives parties facing a tribunal constituted without their proven consent, or amid unaddressed bias objections, a clear route to have the entire arbitration declared void even after interim orders have been passed, and warns institutional claimants against constituting panels unilaterally.

case_name: InterDigital Patent Holdings Inc. & Anr. v. Shenzhen Transsion Holdings Co. Ltd. & Ors.
holding_summary: InterDigital sued Transsion (which sells phones under the Itel, Infinix and Tecno brands) for infringing its Standard Essential Patents covering 3G, 4G, 5G and HEVC video-coding technology, alleging unlicensed use since at least 2016 despite licensing talks since 2019. In a 100-page order — the longest of the Delhi High Court's SEP ad-interim orders — Justice Tushar Rao Gedela directed Transsion to deposit pro tem security with the Registrar General, holding that the threshold for ordering pro tem security is significantly lower than for an interim injunction: prima facie essentiality and validity of the SEPs suffice, and production of comparable licences is not a mandatory precondition.
why_it_matters: The order gives SEP holders a lower evidentiary bar to secure pro tem security from unlicensed implementers early in litigation, without first conclusively proving validity, essentiality or infringement, shaping FRAND litigation strategy in India's growing SEP docket.
